subject: Feature request: vectorize categorical and/or ordered_logistic functions

messages.author: 70a6da99d25bf217
messages.subject: Feature request: vectorize categorical and/or ordered_logistic functions
parts:
Hello,

I'm analyzing a survey that contains several Likert scale items. I model each question as an ordered probit, where the linear predictors depends on covariates and a latent variable that is fixed for an individual. 

To fix ideas, suppose Mik is person i's response to item k which takes values in {1, 2, ..., Jk}. In addition to responses on Mik, I also observe some covariates Xi. I want to estimate the following model:
 
θi | Xi ∼ N(α'Xi, σ)
Pr(Mik = 1 | Xi) = Φ(c1k - βk'Xi + γk θi)
Pr(Mik = 2 | Xi) = Φ(c2k - βk'Xi + γk θi) - Φ(c1k - βk'Xi +-γk θi)
...
Pr(Mik = Jk-1 | Xi) = Φ(cJk - 1, k - βk'Xi + γk θi) - Φ(cJk - 2, k - βk'Xi - γk θi)
Pr(Mik = Jk | Xi) = 1-Φ(cJk, k - βk'Xi - γk θi)
γ1 = 1, ∑k βk = 0 (normalizations to ensure identification)

(priors on α, σ, cjk,βk γk not shown)

I've written a Stan program that can implement this model. However, it runs very slowly. I think the main problem is that it is not possible to vectorize categorical_lpmf(ints y | vector theta) (or ordered_logistic_lpmf(int k | real eta, vector c)) when the parameter vector theta (eta) varies with y (k). All the univariate continuous distributions permit this type of vectorization, as do many of the univariate discrete distributions (e.g. bernoulli, binomial, negative binomial, Poisson). Would it be possible to implement vectorization for these Stan functions?

Thanks very much for your help!

All the best,
David

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature request: vectorize categorical and/or ordered_logistic functions
parts:
Vectorizing everything that's not currently vectorized is near the
top of our to-do list. But in this case, it's not going to help a whole
lot with efficiency because if the categorical parameter varies, there aren't
any computations to share and only a minor reduction in the number of
intermediate nodes in the expression graph and it will remove some virtual
function calls in C++ (which are relatively slow).

We have the ordered logit built in, though that's also not vectorized.
But it should be more efficient than doing an ordered probit by hand.

The other issue that will make Stan slow is poor identification of
parameters or other model misspecifications. You can try with simulated
data to see what fit speed is like if the model matches the data (and
we generally recommend it for debugging).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature request: vectorize categorical and/or ordered_logistic functions
parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for your response! I've had pretty good success with estimation on simulated data, it just takes a few hours. I'll try recoding as an ordered logit and see if that helps. 

Another possible problem is the way I store the probabilities. Currently, I store them in an array of the form

matrix[N,K] probs[c + 1] 

where c is the number of cutoffs and probs[j,i,k] is the probability that person i choose j on item k. From what I understand in the documentation, its difficult to collect probs[1,i,k], ... , probs[c+1,i,k] into a vector because the elements are not contiguous in memory. It seems like it would be better to store them as

vector[c+1] probs[N,K]

However, if I store them this way I can't use matrices to form the probabilities. Instead, I have to loop to fill out the array, which seems inefficient. What do you recommend?

All the best,
David

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature request: vectorize categorical and/or ordered_logistic functions
parts:
It's worth looping to fill in a matrix or vector to allow
matrix arithmetic. The looping and copying itself is basically
free relative to everything else going on (it all gets
compiled to C++ directly). But what you don't want to do
is call distribution functions or other things that create
intermediate expressions if you can use vectorized forms
instead. Vectorizing there will cut down on expression graph
size, which improves speed. There's a chapter of the manual
that discusses optimization.

- Bob
